{{Suharto series}}
The '''Berkeley Mafia''' was the term given to a group of [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California]]-trained<ref name=Bev>{{cite book |last=Bevins |first=Vincent |author-link=Vincent Bevins |date=2020 |title=The Jakarta Method |url= |publisher= |page=182 }}</ref> [[economics|economists]] in [[Indonesia]] who were given [[technocracy|technocratic]] positions under the [[Suharto]] dictatorship during the late 1960s. They were appointed in the early stages of the [[New Order (Indonesia)|New Order]] administration.<ref>{{cite news |last=McCawley |first=Tom |date=28 January 2008 |title= Economic Upside – and Downside |url=http://www.atimes.com/atimes/Southeast_Asia/JA28Ae02.html |url-status=dead |work=[[Asia Times]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080509184752/http://www.atimes.com/atimes/Southeast_Asia/JA28Ae02.html |archive-date=9 May 2008 }}</ref> Their work focused on promoting [[Market economy#Free-market capitalism|free-market capitalism]] in Indonesia and reversing many of the economic reforms that had been introduced by the [[Sukarno]] government, besides that [[Suharto]] claimed that he rejects [[capitalism]],<ref>Soeharto; Dwipayana, G.; Ramadhan, Karta Hadimadja (1991). Soeharto, My Thoughts, Words, and Deeds: An Autobiography. Citra Lamtoro Gung Persada. ISBN 9789798085017.</ref> however later he supported capitalism.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Paundralinga | first1=Angsoka Yorintha | title=Reviewed work: Indonesia Betrayed: How Development Fails, Elizabeth Culler Collins | journal=Asean Economic Bulletin | date=2009 | volume=26 | issue=3 | pages=329–331 | doi=10.1355/AE26-3K | jstor=41317077 | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41317077 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> The economic system in place under the [[New Order (Indonesia)|New Order]] regime was termed [[crony capitalism]] due to the vast corruption within the country throughout this period.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bevins |first=Vincent |author-link=Vincent Bevins |date=2020 |title=The Jakarta Method |url= |publisher= |page=183 }}</ref> The Berkeley Mafia, like the Suharto dictatorship itself, aligned with the [[United States]] during the [[Cold War]].<ref name=Bev/>

While sharing many similarities with the [[Chicago Boys]] in [[Military dictatorship of Chile (1973–1990)|Chile]] (1970s–80s), such as staunch [[anti-communism]], the '''Berkeley Mafia''' was not considered to be [[Neoliberalism|neoliberal]] unlike the former.<ref>{{cite book |last=Bevins |first=Vincent |author-link=Vincent Bevins |date=2020 |title=The Jakarta Method |url= |publisher= |page=207 }}</ref>

The group included [[Widjojo Nitisastro]], [[Mohammad Sadli]], [[Emil Salim]], [[J. B. Sumarlin]], and [[Ali Wardhana]]. [[Dorodjatun Kuntjoro-Jakti]] who graduated later from Berkeley is also sometimes included as a member of this group.

==Origins==
In the mid-1950s, the economists who would become the Berkeley Mafia were students at the Faculty of Economics at the [[University of Indonesia]] (FEUI). The faculty was headed by [[Sumitro Djojohadikusumo]], an economist who had served as [[Ministry of Trade (Indonesia)|Minister of Trade and Industry]] and [[Ministry of Finance (Indonesia)|Minister of Finance]] for the Government. Sumitro was the only teacher with an economics doctorate and so had to turn to foreign lecturers from the [[Netherlands]] and lecturers from other faculties to assist in educating the students at FEUI.<ref name=ford>{{cite web |url=http://www.fordfound.org/elibrary/documents/5002/057.cfm#5002-div2-d0e2149 |title=Ford Foundation: Celebrating Indonesia - 057 |access-date=2007-02-15 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070125064125/http://www.fordfound.org/elibrary/documents/5002/057.cfm#5002-div2-d0e2149 |archive-date=2007-01-25 }}</ref>[[File:Soemitro Smiling.jpg|left|thumb|217x217px|[[Sumitro Djojohadikusumo]] ]]As tensions grew between Indonesia and the Dutch government over West Irian (now known as [[West Papua (region)|West Papua]]), Dutch lecturers began to leave the country. Sumitro turned to the [[Ford Foundation]] for assistance.<ref name=ford/> The Ford Foundation then began a process by which students from the FEUI were chosen to undertake overseas studies at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. After the Ford Foundation had conducted some preliminary preparations, the overseas studies program began in 1957. By the early 1960s, all of the students who had been sent abroad had returned from [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]] and had begun taking up positions as lecturers at the Army Staff and Command College (SESKOAD).<ref name=elson149>{{harv|Elson|2001|p=149}}</ref>

In 1966, General [[Suharto]] took over executive control in Indonesia from President [[Sukarno]] in a coup by virtue of [[Supersemar]]. Although he would not formally become president for another two years, Suharto began laying down the foundations for what would become the [[New Order (Indonesia)|New Order]] regime. In late August 1966, Suharto held a seminar at SESKOAD to discuss political and economic matters and the way in which the New Order would approach those problems. The FEUI economists, headed by [[Widjojo Nitisastro]], attended the seminar.

During the seminar, the economists set out their ideas and policy recommendations. Their presentation impressed Suharto, who invited them to begin work as a team of experts in the field of economics and finance.<ref>{{cite book |last= Dick |first= Howard |title= The Emergence of a National Economy: An Economic History of Indonesia 1800-2000 |publisher= Allen and Unwin |location= Crow's Nest, NSW, Australia |page= 196 |year= 2002|display-authors=etal}}</ref> For his accomplishments, Sumitro Djojohadikusumo was often called the "[[Capo dei capi|Godfather]] of Indonesian economists",<ref>{{Cite book |title=Recollections: the Indonesian economy, 1950s-1990s |date=2003 |publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies |isbn=978-981-230-174-1 |editor-last=Australian National University. Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies |series=Local history and memoirs |location=S.l. |editor-last2=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies |editor-last3=Thee |editor-first3=Kian Wie}}</ref> a title he disliked.<ref>{{Cite web |date=29 March 1999 |title=Sumitro Djojohadikusumo: Saya Bukan Godfather |url=https://www.tempo.co/wawancara/wawancara-sumitro-djojohadikusumo-1027868 |access-date=2026-05-06 |website=Tempo |language=id}}</ref>

== Accomplishments and controversies ==
On October 3, 1966, on the advice of these economists and others, Suharto announced a program aimed at stabilization and rehabilitation of Indonesia's economy.<ref name=elson149 /> The Berkeley Mafia focused on low inflation, fiscal constraint, and market deregulation.<ref name="businessweek">William Pesek, '[https://web.archive.org/web/20100804051011/http://www.businessweek.com/news/2010-03-07/-berkeley-mafia-now-has-514-billion-at-stake-william-pesek.html ‘Berkeley Mafia’ Now Has $514 Billion at Stake]', . BusinessWeek. Accessed February 4, 2010.</ref> The program also aimed at rehabilitation of infrastructure and development of the agricultural sector. At the same time, an international program to support economic recovery was established under the auspices of a newly-formed [[Inter-Governmental Group on Indonesia]].
 
The new economic program was successful at stabilizing the economy. Inflation fell from 650% in 1966 to only 13% in 1969.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.soehartocenter.com/opini/kesaksian/emil_salim.shtml |title=Emil Salim: Pak Harto Selamatkan Bangsa dari Kehancuran {{!}} Soeharto Media Center - Soeharto Review<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2007-02-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070205021805/http://www.soehartocenter.com/opini/kesaksian/emil_salim.shtml |archive-date=2007-02-05 |url-status=dead}}</ref> After Suharto became president in 1968, the members of the Berkeley Mafia team were appointed to ministerial and senior advisory posts in Suharto's cabinet. Thus, the group had a great influence on economic policy and successfully brought Indonesia's economy to an unprecedented growth period. The growth rate was high, averaging around 6.5% per year between the late 1960s and 1997, when South East Asia was hit by the severe [[Asian financial crisis]].<ref name="businessweek" />

The Berkeley Mafia's [[economic liberalism|liberal approach]] towards economics was not supported by everyone. Within the New Order, it encountered opposition from generals such as [[Ali Murtopo]], [[Ibnu Sutowo]] and [[Ali Sadikin]], whose economic approaches were more [[economic nationalism|nationalistic]] in nature.<ref>{{harv|Elson|2001|p=217}}</ref>  Some other groups, like the Indonesian branch of [[Hizb ut-Tahrir]], considered the Berkeley Mafia to be traitors, a view stemming particularly from its willingness to privatise the nation's industries.<ref name="HTI">[http://hizbut-tahrir.or.id/2008/07/08/mafia-berkeley-pengkhianat/ Mafia Berkeley: Pengkhianat!] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170214102722/http://hizbut-tahrir.or.id/2008/07/08/mafia-berkeley-pengkhianat/ |date=2017-02-14 }}. Hizbut-Tahrir Indonesia. Accessed Februari 4, 2011.</ref> With the beginning of the oil boom in the mid-1970s, Suharto favored the economic nationalists and so the Berkeley Mafia's influence was restricted. The Pangaribuan (1995: 248) said later that, [[Suharto]] remained a stubborn [[economic nationalist]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rock |first=Michael T. |title=The Politics of Development Policy and Development Policy Reform in New Order Indonesia |url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/handle/2027.42/40018/wp632.pdf?sequ |website=deepblue.lib.umich.edu}}</ref> Jan P. Wenger  had a different view and wrote that [[Suharto]] embraced [[developmentalism]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wenger |first=Jan P. |title=Petroleum and the Politics of Decolonization in Indonesia: A Study of Economic Development and Nationalism |url=https://digitalcommons.colby.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2425&context=honorstheses |website=digitalcommons.colby.edu}}</ref> Another view is that [[Suharto]] advocated for [[Protectionism|protectionist]] ([[Statism|State-led economics]]) policies, other countries had similar economic policies, some of the leaders of the country saw themselves as [[Third Position]] or as [[Third Way]] advocater, however [[Suharto]] didn't supported the [[Third Position]] or the [[Third Way]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.jeffsachs.org/newspaper-articles/85p6fsamccjl6gmsr6ywtxe9tjl5hj | title=Model That Couldn't | date=23 June 1997 }}</ref>

Suharto would turn to the Berkeley Mafia again in the mid-1980s, when the price of oil began to drop and with it Indonesia's economic growth. The Berkeley Mafia presided over the liberalization, [[deregulation]], and the renewed growth of the Indonesian economy.<ref>{{harv|Elson|2001|p=247}}</ref> Once again, the Indonesian economy began to grow, and once again, the Berkeley Mafia encountered political opposition. This time, their opponents were [[Sudharmono]] and [[Ginandjar Kartasasmita]], who advocated economic nationalism, as well as [[BJ Habibie]], who wanted a technology-centered economic development. As on the previous occasion, Suharto sided with the economic nationalists, and the Berkeley Mafia's power weakened.

During Indonesia's economic collapse from the [[1997 Asian financial crisis]], people blamed the Berkeley Mafia and considered it to be part of the New Order regime. During the Reform era, only [[Widjojo Nitisastro|Widjojo]] was retained in the government.

==Post-Suharto era==
Out of the Berkeley Mafia group, only [[Widjojo Nitisastro]] and [[Emil Salim]] continued to have significant influence within government during the post-Suharto [[Reformation (Indonesia)|Reform era]]. [[Widjojo Nitisastro]] became an economic advisor to presidents [[B. J. Habibie]]. [[B.J. Habibie]] embraced beside this [[Economic nationalism|economic nationalist]] policies,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Richburg |first=Keith B. |date=1998-02-19 |title=Indonesian Oracle, or Oddball? B.J. Habibie Divides a Nation |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1998/02/19/indonesian-oracle-or-oddball-bj-habibie-divides-a-nation/f1386100-06d6-424f-8743-280a89c484ef/ |access-date=2025-06-18 |work=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/1/article/784955/pdf | title=Indonesia and Globalization | journal=Asian Perspective | date=1999 | volume=23 | issue=4 | pages=229–259 | last1=Murphy | first1=Ann Marie | doi=10.1353/apr.1999.0008 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> which [[B.J. Habibie]] called "[[Pancasila-based]] [[Market economy]]".<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.kompas.id/baca/english/2018/02/15/pancasila-based-market-economy | title=Pancasila-based Market Economy | date=15 February 2018 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | chapter-url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/oa-edit/10.1201/9781003534495-56/implementation-pancasila-economic-system-bj-habibie-government-wahyu-hidayat-riyanto-luluk-setyowati-ningsih | doi=10.1201/9781003534495-56 | chapter=Implementation of the Pancasila economic system in Bj. Habibie government | title=Economic Sustainability and Social Equality in the Technological Era | date=2024 | last1=Riyanto | first1=Wahyu Hidayat | last2=Ningsih | first2=Luluk Setyowati | pages=571–577 | isbn=978-1-003-53449-5 }}</ref> [[Abdurrahman Wahid|Wahid (Gus Dur)]], and [[Megawati Sukarnoputri|Megawati]]. [[Emil Salim]] later served as the leader of the [[Presidential Advisory Council]] during [[Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono]]'s administration and also continued to be active on environmental issues, both in Indonesia and in international circles. Mohammad Sadli remained well known as a senior economic commentator until his death in 2008.<ref>Hal Hill and [[Thee Kian Wie]] (2008), 'Moh. Sadli (1922-2008), economist, minister and public intellectual', ''[[Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies]]'', 4 (1), April, pp. 151-156.</ref>

As of today, Emil Salim and Dorodjatun Kuntjoro-Jakti are two surviving member of the Berkeley Mafia.
